mechaber.he:
הלוקח כלים מן האומן למכור. ובו ב סעיפים:
הלוקח כלים מבית האומן לשגרן לבית חמיו ואמר לו אם מקבלים אותן ממני אתן לך דמיהם ואם לאו אתן לך שכר מועט ונאנסו בהליכה חייב ואם נאנסו בחזרה פטור אבל אם נגנבו או אבדו חייב:
mechaber.en: Take tools from the artist to sell. And in clauses: Taking the tools from the trained house to send them to the house of his brothers and telling him if you receive them from me, I will give you a fee and give you a little wage and be raped by a walk, and if we try back is exempt, but if they are stolen or lost, they must:

baer_hetev.he: פטור. דהרי גילה דעתו שאם לא יקבלו ממנו יחזירם להאומן והרי לא קבלו ובשביל ההנאה שהראה בבית חמיו הוא נותן לו שכר מועט מש"ה אין לו דין שואל אלא דין שוכר שחייב בגניבה ואבידה כמ"ש בר"ס ש"ז עכ"ל הסמ"ע ועיין בתשו' ן' לב ס"ג סי' פ"א:
baer_hetev.en: exempt. Deri thought that if he did not get him back to the artist, and he did not receive and for the pleasure he showed in his house, he gave him a small wage than he did not ask, but rather an exclaimer that he had to do so and confessed as a lawyer

beer_hagolah.he:
א) ל' הרמב"ם פ"ב מה' שלוחין דין ח' מברייתא ב"מ דף פ"א ע"א וכתבה הרי"ף בפ' השואל
ב) לשון הברייתא לסי' טובת הנאה שבהם כלומר שיחזיקו לו טובה שפקדתים בסבלונות
ג) פי' רש"י הואיל וקץ דמים ומשכם לשם לקיחה הרי הם כלקוחים וכ"כ הגהות שם שגם ר"י הסכים לדברי רש"י ול' הברייתא מסייעתם דבקץ דמי' עסקינן שא"ל אתן לך דמיהן משמע שכבר היו קצובין ואין מדברי רבינו הכרע וכ"כ הכ"מ
ד) עוד וכן הוא בברייתא בנוסחאות שלפנינו והכי דייק לישנא דרבינו
beer_hagolah.en:
The language of Rambam, chapter 2 of Hilkhot Sheluchin, law 8, from the baraita in Bava Metzia 81a, cited by Rif in HaSho'el.
The baraita's wording refers to "the benefit of gratitude contained in them," meaning that the recipients will be grateful to him for sending them gift items.
Rashi explains that since the price was fixed and he took the items for the purpose of purchase, they are considered purchased. Hagahot Maimoniyot likewise writes that Ri agreed with Rashi. The wording of the baraita supports them, because it speaks where the price was fixed, saying, "I will give you their value," implying the value had already been set. Rambam's own wording does not conclusively decide this point, as Kesef Mishneh writes.
This too appears in the baraita in the textual versions before us, and Rambam's wording supports that reading.

beur_hagra.he: אם נגנבו כו'. שם תנ"ה כו' כנושא שכר וכן פי' הרמב"ן והרא"ש והר"ן:
beur_hagra.en: If they were stolen, etc. There the baraita likewise teaches, etc., that he is like a paid custodian. Ramban, Rosh, and Ran explain accordingly.

chokhmat_shlomo.he: סעיף א' ואני אתן לך שכר מועט. נ"ב עיין בסמ"ע שהביא לשון הטור ואני אתן לך שכר הנאה וכו'. והנה באמת כן הוא לשון הש"ס בברייתא אני נותן לך כפי טובת הנאה שבהם. אך עיין בחיבורי לנדרים נקרא נדרי זריזין שם העלתי דבכוונה שינה הרמב"ם הלשון. והדין הוא כך דבאם משלם דמי כל הטובת הנאה שהוא נהנה אז אינו חייב באונסין רק בזבינא חריפא. אבל בזבינא מצעי פטור מאונסין אבל אם נותן לו רק שכר מועט לא כפי שוויו של טובת הנאה שנהנה רק פחות מדמיו בזבינא מציעא. נעשה שואל וחייב באונסין. ומיושב בזה מה שתמה המל"מ בפ"ב מה' שלוחין בזה על הרמב"ם עיי"ש והבן: ועוד כתבנו יישוב אחר בזה די"ל דבאונס לבדו אף בזבינא מציעא חייב בההוא הנאה דנותן לו לבקרו או לקנותו על הספק אם ירצו בית חמיו או לא נעשה שואל וחייב באונסין אך במתה מחמת מלאכה יש חילוק דאם הוא זבינא חריפא נעשה אף לוקח וחייב אף במתה מחמת מלאכה ואם הוא זבינא מציעא פטור במתה מחמת מלאכה ודינה לשאר שואל עיי"ש בחיבורי נדרי זרוזין ותבין מילתא בטעמא. ועיין מ"ש בזה לקמן בסימן רי"ש סעיף יו"ד גם בסרסור ל"ב חריפא זבינא לענין אונסין דבההיא הנאה שנותן לו על הספק מתחייב באונסין ורק לענין מחמת מלאכה בעינן זבינא חריפא ומיושב קושית התו' בב"מ דף פ"א עיי"ש: @33לסימן @33הנ"ל. עיין בסמ"ע ס"ק כ"ו בהג"ה מ"ש. כתב בהגהות מרדכי כל שכירות פועל א"צ קנין. ועיין בתשו' מוהרי"ט ח"ב חלק חו"מ סי' נ"ג והביאו המשל"מ בה' איסורי מזבח פ"ד הלכה י"ג ומ"ש שם בשם הרא"ש במס' ע"ז ר"פ השוכר את הפועל ועיין מ"ש בתשובה אחרת לחקור בדין היכא דשייך דין קלבד"מ אם נמי חל החיוב בדבור או לא. ונ"מ לענין לחייב לצי"ש או לענין תפיסה עיי"ש מ"ש בזה ובדיני אתנן:
chokhmat_shlomo.en: Seif 1: “And I will give you a small wage.” Note: The Sema cites the Tur's wording, “I will give you payment corresponding to the benefit.” The baraita indeed says that he will pay according to the benefit received. I have explained elsewhere that Rambam intentionally changed the wording. If the recipient pays the full value of the benefit he receives, he is liable for unavoidable accidents only where the merchandise is especially easy to sell. With ordinary merchandise he is exempt from accidents. But if he pays only a small wage, less than the value of the benefit, then even with ordinary merchandise he is treated as a borrower and is liable for accidents. I offered another resolution. Even with ordinary merchandise, the benefit of being permitted to inspect or conditionally take the item can make him a borrower for ordinary accidents. The distinction between especially marketable and ordinary merchandise may instead concern loss caused through normal use. With especially marketable goods he is treated also as a purchaser and is liable even where the item dies through its permitted use; with ordinary goods he retains the ordinary borrower's exemption for loss caused by the work itself. This also resolves Tosafot's difficulty in Bava Metzia 81. Regarding the Sema's citation of Hagahot Mordechai that hiring a worker requires no formal kinyan, see the authorities I cited elsewhere. I have also discussed whether, where the principle of kim lei bid'rabba minei prevents judicial collection, the wage obligation nevertheless takes effect through speech for purposes of a moral obligation or seizure. The same question arises in the laws of prohibited payment.

meirat_einayim.he:
אתן לך שכר מועט. ל' הטור אתן לך שכר כפי מה שנהנה בו שהראה בבית חמיו שהיה חפץ לשלוח להן דורון:
בהליכה חייב דהואיל שקצץ עם המוכר דמיו ולקחן הרי הם לקוחין בידו עד שידע שלא יקבלו ממנו בבית חמיו:
בחזרה פטור. פי' מן האונסין דהרי גילה דעתו מתחלה שבאם לא ירצה לקבלו ממנו יחזירהו ליד האומן והרי לא קבלו ואי משום ההנאה שהראה בו בבית חמיו הרי הוא עכ"פ נותן להאומן כפי הנאה מ"ה אין לו דין שואל אלא דין שוכר שחייב בגניבה ואביד' כמו שכיר וכמ"ש הטור והמחבר לקמן ר"ס ש"ז ע"ש:
meirat_einayim.en:
I give you a little wage. “The column gives you a salary like what you have seen in the house of his brothers who would like to send them a doron:
In walking, Douil must be decorated with the seller, his blood, and he shall take him in his hand until he knows that he will not receive him in his warm house:
Back to exemption. P. From the rape of Deri, his opinion revealed that if he did not want to receive him from him, he would not receive and not because of the pleasure he saw in the house of his brothers, he would give him an artist as a pleasure, “He does not have a lawyer, but rather an employer who must be treated like a bribe and a friend of the columnist.”

netivot_hamishpat_beurim.he: ונאנסו בהליכה חייב. הוא לשון הרמב"ם ובמל"מ תמה דבפ"ד מה' מכירה גבי לוקח כלים ע"מ לבקרן כתב הרמב"ם דבעינן קייצי וזבינא חריפ' וכדמוכח בנדרים דף ל"א וכאן לא הזכיר שום חילוק ע"ש והנה הא דלא הזכיר קייצי ל"ק כמ"ש הש"מ ב"מ ד' פ"א דבלוקח ע"מ לשגרן מסתם משמע דקצץ דמי והיינו דהיאך יקח לשגרן לחמיו אם לא יקצץ דמים דאולי אם יוכשר בעיני חמיו פן יפסוק המוכר דמים ביוקר עד שלא יהי' באפשרי ליקח אותם משא"כ בלבקרו איכא למיטעי שלקחו לבקרו קודם קציצת דמים לכך הוצרך להתנות שיהי' בדקייצי דמי אבל הא ודאי קשה דלמה לא התנה הרמב"ם דבעינן זבינא חריפא עוד הקשה בלח"מ דהדיוקים סתרי שכתב הדין דבזבינא חריפא חייב באונסין ומשמע דבזבינא מציעא פטור מאונסין (וכן האמת מוכח בנדרים ל"א) ולבסוף כתב דבזבינא דרמיא על אפיה פטור ומשמע דזבינ' מציעא חייב באונסין ועוד ק"ל על המחבר דבכאן פירש זבינא חריפא האמור בש"ס ביש לו קונים הרבה ובסי' ר' מפרש זבינא חריפא שחביב על הלוקח. וליישב כ"ז נראה דהנה בתוס' ורא"ש דחקו עצמם בהא דמוכח בנדרים דחיוב אונסין הוא מטעם שואל דהא מצריך שיהי' רק הנאת לוקח ולא הנאת מוכר ובב"ב דף פ"ח מוכח דחיוב אונסין הוא מטעם לוקח ובשטה בב"מ דף פ"א מחלק דבקייצא דמים ואינו זבינא חריפא החיוב הוא מטעם לוקח ובזבינא חריפא ולא קייצי דמים היא מטעם שואל ע"ש והנה הא דבקייצי חייב מטעם לוקח מסתבר כדבריו דודאי נגד החיוב שהוא מצד לוקח אף שיש בו גם כן הנאת מוכר חייב וא"צ שיהיה הנאת לוקח לבד אבל מ"ש דבזבינא חריפא אף דלא קייצי הוי שואל הוא תמוה מאוד דהא מבואר בנדרים דכשלוקח ביותר משוויו אף פ"א לא הוי שוב זבינא חריפא וכיון דלא קייצי ממילא שוב לא נחשב זבינא חריפא דאולי הוא ביוקר ולכן מסתבר ליה להרמב"ם דבקייצי ודאי הוי לוקח אף בזבינא מציעא אבל שואל לא הוי עד שיהיה זבינא חריפא גם כן דליכא רק הנאת לוקח ולא הנאת מוכר וכל הנאה שלו ואז הוי שואל וחיוב הוא מטעם שניהם דהיינו מטעם לוקח ומטעם שואל והנ"מ בהא דחייב גם כן מטעם שואל הוא דהנה הרשב"א והרא"ש כתבו דבלוקח ע"מ לבקרן אפילו אחר שגילה דעתו דלא ניחא ליה חייב באונסין וכתב הב"י הטעם דכל שואל חייב באחריות עד שיחזור ליד המשאיל ע"ש (ועמ"ש בסמוך דכשגילה דעתו שלא בפני המוכר דכ"ע מודים דחייב באונסין וטעם זה שייך בשואל אבל כשהחיוב הוא מטעם לוקח לבד דהוא מטעם כיון שאין המוכר יכול לחזור בו אבל אחר שגילה דעתו שאינו רוצה בו ונתבטל משיכתו הראשונה ודאי דאף המוכר יכול לחזור בו ובטל שם לוקח ממנו וכמו בלוקח על תנאי דכשנתברר שנתבטל התנאי דאין לו שם לוקח שוב ובזה אתי שפיר הסוגי' דנדרים דמוכח משמואל דהנאת לוקח לבד הוא ולא הנאת מוכר דמשמע מדברי שמואל דחייב באונסין אף לאחר שגילה דעתו כמ"ש הרמב"ם וע"כ מטעם חיוב שואל הוא שכל הנאה של לוקח הוא ומש"ה מוקי ליה בזבינא חריפא דוקא דאז הוא רק הנאת לוקח ולא של מוכר לבד כתב הרמב"ם דין דזבינא חריפא גם כן גבי הלוקח על מנת לבקרו מה שאין כן בפ"ב משלוחין גבי לוקח כלים לשגרן לבית חמיו דבאמת אינו חייב רק בהליכ' ולא בחזר' ובהליכה קודם שיש גילוי דעת. דלא ניחא ליה החיוב הוא אפי' כשהוא מטעם לוקח לבד ולא שואל לכך חייב בקייצי לבד אף שאינו זבינ' חריפ' ולפ"ז ל"ק ג"כ הדיוקים אהדדי מה שהקשה הלח"מ דמתחל' כתב דינא דשמואל דחייב באונסין אפי' אחר שגילה דעתו וזה הוא רק בזבינא חריפא דליכא רק הנאת לוקח ולא הנאת מוכר משום חיוב שואל נגע בו ובזביני דרמי על אפי' כתב הרמב"ם דפטור לגמרי אפי' קודם גילוי דעת דאין לו אפי' דין לוקח כלל דלא סמכה דעתו כלל שיקחנ' משא"כ בזבינ' מציע' דיש בו הנאת לוקח והנאת מוכר הוא דין אמצעי שהוא רק חייב מטעם לוקח ולא מטעם שואל ואינו חייב רק בהליכה ולא בחזר' דהיינו אחר שגילה דעתו ולא כתבו הרמב"ם משום שאין דרכו של הרמב"ם לכתוב דין מה שאינו מפורש בש"ס. אמנם בהא דלשגרן אף בזבינ' דרמי על אפי' חייב בהליכה מטעם לוקח והטעם דדוקא בלוקח לבקרן ובשוויין (דבלוקח בפחות הוא אפי' שואל כדמוכח בנדרים שם) כשהוא זבינא דרמי על אפי' קרוב לודאי שלא יקחנו משא"כ בלוקח לשגרן לחמיו במתנ' שהוא כבר לקחן לגמרי רק שהוא על תנאי אם ירצה חמיו לקבל המתנה אפי' בזבינא דרמי על אפי' חשיב לוקח דסמכא דעתי' שבודאי יקבלנו חמיו במתנה. ולזה בסי' ר' שהביא המחבר דעת הרמב"ם מביא פי' הרמב"ם בזבינ' חריפא דהיינו שיהיה החפץ חביב על הלוקח משא"כ כאן בהא דהלוקח ע"מ לשגרן או ע"מ למוכרן שהביא דעת הי"א שהוא דעת הרא"ש ע"כ הוצרך להביא ג"כ פי' הרא"ש דהיינו שיש לו קונים רבים דבע"מ לשגרן לחמיו ובע"מ למוכרם ודאי דלא תליא בהמקח במה שחביב על הלוקח דהא אינו תלוי בדעתו כלל רק בדעת אחרים והוכרח לפרש לדינו של הרא"ש פירושו של הרא"ש דהיינו שיש לו קונים רבים:
netivot_hamishpat_beurim.en: And they were lost through ones while going, he is liable. This is Rambam's language. Mishneh LaMelech asks that in chapter 4 of Hilchot Mechirah, concerning one who takes utensils in order to inspect them, Rambam requires both a fixed price and a readily marketable item, as is evident from Nedarim 31. Here he records no such conditions. The omission of a fixed price is not difficult. Shitah Mekubetzet in Bava Metzia 81 explains that one who takes items in order to send them to his father-in-law is ordinarily understood to have fixed the price beforehand. How could he take an item to present to his father-in-law without knowing its price? Perhaps the father-in-law will like it and the seller will then demand an unaffordable price. By contrast, one who merely takes an item to inspect it may reasonably do so before price is fixed, and therefore Rambam had to state expressly that the price was fixed in that case. The real difficulty is why Rambam does not require that the item be readily marketable. Lechem Mishneh further asks that Rambam's implications contradict one another. At first he says that with a readily marketable item the buyer is liable for ones, implying that with an ordinary item he is exempt. This is in fact evident from Nedarim 31. But at the end Rambam says that with merchandise that is difficult to sell he is exempt, which implies that an ordinary item carries liability. I am also troubled by Mechaber, who here explains "readily marketable" as an item with many potential buyers, while in siman 200 he explains it as an item especially desirable to this buyer. The matter can be resolved as follows. Tosafot and Rosh struggle with the fact that Nedarim shows liability for ones to be based on the law of a borrower, because it requires the benefit to belong only to the buyer and not to the seller, whereas Bava Batra 88 implies that liability is based on his status as buyer. Shitah Mekubetzet in Bava Metzia 81 distinguishes: where the price is fixed but the item is not particularly marketable, liability is based on buyer status; where it is particularly marketable but the price is not fixed, liability is based on borrower status. The first part is compelling. Once the price is fixed, he can indeed have the law of a buyer even though the seller too benefits. Buyer liability does not require exclusive benefit to the buyer. But the second part is difficult. If the price is not fixed, how can the item be considered especially attractive to the buyer? Nedarim itself shows that if the seller demands more than market value, the item ceases to be "readily marketable" even to that buyer. Without a fixed price, perhaps the seller will demand an excessive amount. Rambam therefore appears to hold that when the price is fixed, even an ordinary item gives the holder the status of a buyer. He becomes a borrower only when the item is also especially marketable, so that the entire benefit lies with him and not with the seller. Thus two bases of liability can coexist: buyer liability and borrower liability. A practical difference appears after he reveals that he does not want the item. Rashba and Rosh write that one who takes an item to inspect it remains liable for ones even after revealing that he does not want it. Beit Yosef explains that every borrower remains responsible until the object returns to the lender. This rationale applies to borrower liability. But where liability rests only on buyer status, the basis is that the seller cannot retract during the relevant period. Once the holder announces that he does not want the item, the original meshichah as a prospective buyer is canceled. The seller can now take the item back, and the holder no longer has buyer status. This resembles a conditional purchase in which the condition fails. Therefore the liability based solely on buyer status ends when he gives notice. This resolves the sugya in Nedarim. Shmuel's ruling implies that the holder remains liable even after revealing that he does not want the item. That can only be because he has borrower liability, meaning the entire benefit is his. Therefore the Gemara establishes the case specifically with an especially marketable item. Rambam accordingly records the condition of a readily marketable item in the law of one who takes an item to inspect, because he is addressing Shmuel's rule of continuing liability after notice. For that, borrower status is necessary. But in chapter 2 of Hilchot Sheluchin, concerning one who takes items to send to his father-in-law, Rambam says he is liable only on the outward journey, not on the return. During the outward journey, before he has revealed dissatisfaction, buyer liability alone suffices. Since the price is assumed fixed, he is liable even if the item is ordinary. No special marketability is needed. This also resolves Lechem Mishneh's conflicting implications. Rambam's first statement about an especially marketable item concerns Shmuel's rule, liability even after notice, and therefore requires borrower status. Rambam's later statement that an item difficult to sell is exempt even earlier means that such an item does not even create buyer status, because the holder never reasonably expects to keep it. An ordinary item occupies the middle category: during the outward journey he is liable as a buyer, but after revealing dissatisfaction he is no longer liable for ones because he was never a borrower. There is also a difference between one who takes an item to inspect and one who takes it to send as a gift. If he takes an ordinary item at its market price merely to inspect it, and the item is generally difficult to sell, it is close to certain he will not buy it. He therefore does not acquire buyer status. But one who takes the item as a gift for his father-in-law has already taken it substantially as a completed purchase, subject only to the condition whether his father-in-law will accept the gift. Even if the merchandise itself is difficult to sell, the holder has strong reason to expect that his father-in-law will accept it as a gift. He therefore has buyer status on the outward journey. This also explains the different definitions of "readily marketable." In siman 200, where Mechaber cites Rambam's rule regarding one who takes an item to inspect it, the relevant question is whether the object is especially desirable to this buyer, because borrower liability depends on whether the entire benefit is his. Here, however, the cited opinion is Rosh's view concerning taking goods to send or resell. In that context the relevant idea is commercial marketability, whether there are many ready purchasers, because the holder's intention depends on the likelihood that the third party will accept or that he can resell the goods. Mechaber therefore had to adopt Rosh's own interpretation for Rosh's rule.

Even on the return. See Sema, seif katan 4, who gives the reason that the return of this journey is itself part of the outward journey. This comes from the Gemara. At first glance it is difficult according to Rashbam and Rosh, who hold that one who takes an item for inspection remains liable for ones even after revealing that he does not want it, until he actually returns it to the seller. Beit Yosef asks from the case of one who takes goods to send to his father-in-law, where he is exempt from ones on the return, and answers that there he receives compensation if the father-in-law does not accept the goods, and this weakens his borrower status. If so, why is the special rationale that "the return of this journey is part of the outward journey" needed here? The principal here does not pay the sender compensation, so even without that rationale the sender should remain liable for ones until actual return, like one who takes an item for inspection. There are further difficulties. Shitah Mekubetzet in Bava Metzia 81, in the name of Tosafot of Sens, asks how the Gemara proves that after the days of borrowing expire the custodian becomes a paid custodian because "since he benefited, he provides benefit," from the law of one who takes goods to send. Tosafot of Sens asks that there the holder is a true renter because he pays the seller compensation if the gift is rejected. Shitah answers that during the return the rental period has already ended. But immediately before that Shitah cites Ritva that a paid custodian remains liable until he informs the owner, proving this from an artisan. If so, the question returns: why is the holder no longer a renter during the return merely because the gift was rejected, unless he informed the seller? Beit Yosef in siman 200 also asks against the poskim who hold that once the buyer reveals dissatisfaction he is exempt from ones, from the case of the flask sent with a child, where the sender remains liable even after returning it to the child and thereby revealing that he does not want it. A fourth difficulty arises from the Yerushalmi cited by Beit Yosef in Tur, siman 343, concerning one who borrowed today and rented tomorrow, with a question about the intervening night. The version cited there appears contrary to Rashba's version of the Yerushalmi at the beginning of HaShoel, and Rashba's explanation is itself difficult. The case certainly concerns borrowing during the day and not at night, yet the distinction the Yerushalmi draws concerning the night is hard to understand. The matter can be reconciled by distinguishing a loan for a fixed period from a loan for completion of a task. Where an object is borrowed for a fixed time, borrower liability ends when the fixed period ends. The end date itself is like advance notice from the lender that at that time he will take back his property. It is as though the lender had said, "At the end of the term, return my property." The same applies to a renter when the rental period ends. But where one borrows or rents an object to perform a particular task, he remains borrower or renter until he returns it, or until he says, "Take your property," or at least informs the owner that the task is complete. This resembles an artisan, who remains a paid custodian until he says, "I have finished." Once the fixed borrowing term ends, the borrower does not become completely exempt. He becomes a paid custodian because "since he benefited, he provides benefit," as the Gemara explains. This is different from an ordinary paid custodian whose fixed custody term ends. A paid custodian may remain liable so long as the deposit remains with him and he continues to receive his pay, unless he gives notice. Borrower and renter, however, use the item for their own benefit. When their known use period ends, they are no longer permitted to use it without the owner's consent. That itself marks the end of borrower or renter status. Now suppose one borrows for one task and afterward rents for a second task. Once the first task ends, he need not notify the owner in order for the rental phase to begin, because the owner already instructed that after completion of the borrowing task he should continue holding the item under the rental arrangement. This is no different from the owner saying, "When the borrowing period ends, give the item to that renter," and telling the borrower to hand it over. If the designated renter is the same person, no separate notice is necessary. This explains the Yerushalmi concerning borrowing today and renting tomorrow. If animals ordinarily spend the night in the owner's stable, then when the borrowing day ends the night is naturally a time when the item should have returned to the owner. The end of the borrowing day is therefore like the lender saying, "Take your property," and borrower liability has ended. But in a place where borrowed animals are not ordinarily returned at night, the borrowing responsibility continues through the night, because the general rule is that borrower liability does not end until the time at which the owner would normally retake possession. This also reconciles Rashbam and Rosh with the other authorities. When they write that even after the holder reveals dissatisfaction he remains liable for ones, they must mean that he revealed it before witnesses or to third parties but did not inform the seller himself. Such a private declaration does not end the seller's reliance on him, any more than an artisan's private statement before witnesses that his work is complete. By contrast, the authorities who say that revealing dissatisfaction ends liability mean that he communicated this to the seller. That is equivalent to saying, "Take your property," and ends borrower liability. The flask sent with the child is no difficulty. Returning it to the child is not notifying the seller. Delivering it to a minor is no better than declaring before witnesses that one no longer wants it. So long as the seller himself has not been informed and the item has not been returned to him, the holder remains liable. This also resolves the proof in Bava Metzia concerning a borrower becoming a paid custodian after the borrowing period. The Gemara proves from the fact that the holder remains a paid custodian even after he informed the seller and the borrower liability had ended. Thus it must be that after borrowing ends, the former borrower still has paid-custodian liability because he previously benefited. The fact that he had earlier been a renter or received some compensating benefit does not itself explain the continuing liability. Finally, the Gemara's statement here that "the return of this journey is part of the outward journey" is necessary because, unlike a trip to a particular identified recipient such as one's father-in-law, the purpose here is to sell the goods generally. Even after the holder fails to sell them in one location and informs the owner of that failure, the commercial mission has not necessarily ended. He may still sell them on the return journey, even at the door of his own house. The return is therefore still part of the selling mission itself. For that reason he remains liable as on the outward journey, notwithstanding notice that he could not sell in the place to which he first traveled.
And he is liable only for theft and loss. This is difficult to me. This "some say" is plainly the view of Tosafot and Rosh, and according to them the same law should apply even to the first clause concerning one who takes goods to send to his father-in-law. If so, Mechaber should have explained that under this view, when the merchandise is not readily marketable, the holder is only an unpaid custodian on the return journey. Bava Metzia 81 proves that after the borrowing period ends the holder becomes a paid custodian because "since he benefited, he provides benefit." Shitah Mekubetzet asks that in the goods-sent-to-the-father-in-law case the holder pays compensation and is therefore already a paid custodian. It answers that once the father-in-law rejects the goods, the period of that rental has ended. The remaining paid-custodian liability exists only because he had previously been a borrower. Accordingly, where the merchandise is difficult to sell and the holder was never a borrower in the first place, he should be entirely exempt from paid-custodian liability on the return, and have only the law of an unpaid custodian. Even according to what I wrote above, that the Gemara's proof concerns the period after notice to the seller, while before such notice a different rationale could sustain paid-custodian status, the same difficulty remains. Once he has notified the seller, he should at least become only an unpaid custodian under this view. Mechaber should have stated this explicitly.

Between back and walking Dalai is a back model that can sell a signal:
And he does not need to do so, and he does not believe in Hashem’s mercy, and he is not a sinner
He does not need to be raped because he has no pleasure
